claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films or nanoribbons have a high lattice-defect density.
The as-deposited films or nanoribbons contain substantial internal strain or residual stress.
Defects and internal strain produce an irregular magnetic-domain distribution in the as-deposited material.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can relieve internal stress without causing significant grain growth.
Annealing reduces lattice defects in nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type films.
Annealing relaxes internal strain in nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type films.
Reduced defect density and relaxed strain lead to a more uniform magnetic-domain distribution.
Internal stresses and defect sites act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Removing pinning centers facilitates smoother magnetic phase transitions.
Reduced domain-wall pinning lowers magnetic hysteresis.
Annealing improves the reversible magnetocaloric effect.
Annealing enables more efficient heat transfer across the nanoscale structure.
Annealed samples will have a lower hysteresis width than otherwise identical as-deposited controls.
Annealed samples will exhibit a greater reversible temperature change at low applied field than as-deposited controls.
As-deposited films or nanoribbons exhibit high magnetic hysteresis.
As-deposited films or nanoribbons have a diminished magnetocaloric response.
The diminished baseline magnetocaloric response and high hysteresis are caused by defect- and strain-mediated impediments to domain-wall motion.
The predicted annealing effects apply only at low applied fields and temperatures near the magnetic transition.
Interfacial effects at reduced dimensions may alter the benefits of annealing.

Failure of annealing to produce both a statistically significant hysteresis-width reduction and a measurable reversible magnetocaloric enhancement relative to an unannealed control would falsify the hypothesis.
